newsitem.title: BELGIUM: OECD applauds Belgium EMU effort but warns on jobs.
newsitem.headline: OECD applauds Belgium EMU effort but warns on jobs.

text.p: Belgium has probably done enough to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU) but remains blighted by an inefficient labour market that should be reformed, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said on Tuesday.

"While over the past few years joining EMU from its inception has been the overriding priority of the Belgian authorities, it should now be possible to shift progressively the focus of attention to the remaining major problem, namely non-employment," the OECD said in its first country survey on Belgium since September 1995.

The OECD forecast Belgium's government would succeed in bringing its deficit below the Maastricht criterion of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997, the reference year for EMU membership, which will be decided in early 1998.

It forecast the 1997 deficit should fall to 2.9 percent from 3.2 percent in 1996 and reach 2.7 percent in 1998. GDP growth should accelerate to 2.2 percent in 1997 from 1.3 percent in 1996 and reach 2.6 percent in 1998.
The European Commission is due to release its spring economic forecast for 1997 and 1998 on Wednesday.

The OECD said government efforts to clean up public finances had been rewarded and enhanced by a collapse in interest rates (down 150 basis points since mid-1995 at both the short- and long-end), helping Belgium cut the cost of servicing its huge debt.
The OECD said, however, Belgium's unemployment record and regulations in some key sectors of the economy were a point of concern and recommended a series of policy steps the government should take.

Unemployment in Belgium, measured on the OECD's standardised basis, was stable around 9.5 percent of the population, around the European average. But the number of people in work as a percentage of the working population was, at 55 percent in 1995, one of the lowest rates in the OECD area.

The OECD said the government's 1996 law on competitiveness and employment, pushed through parliament using special powers and which is currently under review, should be phased out in favour of measures tackling labour market rigidities.
"These rigidities largely reflect the wage setting process, which should be liberalised - a particularly urgent task, in view of EMU," the OECD said.

Among other measures, it called for the reduction in the "bewildering number" of employment programmes, restricting or abolishing sectoral wage agreements and loosening employment protection legislation.

"Also, to enhance labour mobility and reduce mismatches, fiscal and notary real estate transaction fees should be reduced - a measure which could have a significant impact given the number of Belgian households owning a dwelling," the OECD said.
The OECD said Belgium also needed to introduce more competition into certain sectors, such as distribution and electricity.
